name: Subaru TR580
fullName: Subaru Lineartronic TR580 chain-belt CVT with torque converter and AWD transfer clutch
summary: A chain-belt CVT: a lock-up converter drives a forward/reverse planetary, which feeds a pair of hydraulically squeezed pulleys linked by a steel chain. A transfer clutch in the tail sends torque to the rear axle. The hard parts are unloading the spring-loaded secondary pulley to free the chain and putting every pulley and transfer shim back in place. Fluid level is only right when checked hot at a fixed temperature. In practice many shops replace the variator, valve body or whole unit instead of overhauling it.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: Chain-belt CVT with lock-up torque converter and AWD transfer clutch

facts.label: Generation
facts.value: Second-generation TR580 (Forester SJ, also 2012+ Impreza and FB25 Legacy/Outback)

facts.label: Forward/reverse
facts.value: Planetary with forward clutch and reverse brake, ahead of the primary pulley

facts.label: Oil pump
facts.value: Chain-driven from the converter at about 1.33:1 engine speed

facts.label: Valve body
facts.value: On top of the case under a cover; six solenoids; sold by Subaru only as an assembly

facts.label: Fluid level check
facts.value: Engine idling, CVTF at 35–45 °C, level to bottom of filler hole

facts.label: Front differential
facts.value: Separate 75W-90 GL-5 gear oil, about 1.35–1.4 L

facts.label: Clutch clearances
facts.value: Forward 1.10–1.40 mm, reverse 2.30–2.70 mm, transfer 0.7–1.1 mm

facts.label: Warranty
facts.value: CVT coverage extended to 10 yr/100,000 mi on 2014–15 Forester

notes: Be honest with yourself about scope: Subaru does not sell a variator overhaul, its fix for confirmed chain slip is a complete CVT, and the valve body is sold only as an assembly. Many shops install a new or remanufactured CVT, or replace only the valve body in the car, rather than doing the full bench overhaul learned here.
Chain and pulleys are one decision. Scored sheaves ruin a new chain, so damaged variator parts are replaced as a set, and when they are hard to get the job usually becomes a unit swap.
The torque converter is normally replaced with a new or remanufactured unit or sent to a converter rebuilder, not reused after a debris failure.

Special tool: the secondary pulley has to be held open to remove or fit the chain. The factory expander tool is reported discontinued in the US, so rebuilders make a plate-and-all-thread tool. Never put fingers between the sheaves while it is loaded.

One-time-use parts called out by Subaru include the stator support sealing ring, the differential side (axle) seals, the axle C-clips and the filler plug gasket. A rebuild kit adds the gaskets, seals, sealing rings and frictions.

Clutch clearances and stack-ups come from an aftermarket teardown of the second-generation unit, not factory text. Most torque values are not publicly sourced, so steps say 'torque to spec' rather than give a number.
The valve body is on top of the case on this unit, which is why it can be replaced in the car.

Step count is 114, inside the 90–120 target. Pulley disassembly (sheave seals, the secondary pulley spring) is left out because public sources don't document it for this generation and shops replace pulleys as assemblies.
After any rebuild, valve body or TCM work, clear the AT learning data and run the learning procedure with a Subaru-capable scan tool, or shift quality and lock-up will be wrong.

phases.name: Prep and removal
phases.summary: Record the faults, drain both fluids, pull the CVT and get it on the bench clean.

phases.name: External teardown
phases.summary: Strip the converter, top valve body, AWD extension case, pan, linkage and front pump drive.

phases.name: Internal teardown
phases.summary: Split the case, unload the variator, then remove the forward/reverse unit and final drive.

phases.name: Clean and inspect
phases.summary: Judge the chain, pulleys, clutches, pump, valve body and gears, and decide what gets replaced.

phases.name: Subassembly rebuild
phases.summary: Rebuild the pump and the three clutch packs and set their clearances off the case.

phases.name: Final assembly
phases.summary: Rebuild the unit in reverse order, with the variator, shims and seals placed exactly.

phases.name: Fill, learn and test
phases.summary: Install, fill to a hot level check, clear and redo TCM learning, then prove it on the road.

steps.title: Scan and record CVT codes
steps.action: Before anything is unplugged, read and save every TCM trouble code and a short data log of engine, primary pulley and secondary pulley speeds.
steps.why: The codes and speed traces tell you whether you are chasing chain slip, a solenoid circuit or a converter problem, which decides how deep the rebuild goes.
tools: Subaru Select Monitor (SSM) or equivalent scan tool

mistakes.title: Clearing codes before recording them
mistakes.what: Clears the trouble codes or disconnects the battery before the codes, their current or past status and the freeze-frame data are saved.
mistakes.consequence: The evidence that separates a wiring, sensor or solenoid fault from a hard-part failure is gone, so the depth of the rebuild becomes a guess.
mistakes.prevent: Save the full code list, mark each code current or past, and save the freeze-frame pressures before anything is cleared or unplugged.

mistakes.title: Calling an engine surge chain slip
mistakes.what: Decides the chain is slipping from an rpm flare or vibration without graphing engine, primary pulley and secondary pulley speeds.
mistakes.consequence: An engine-side torque fluctuation gets blamed on the CVT, the unit is torn down or replaced, and the original complaint is still there afterward.
mistakes.prevent: Duplicate the complaint while recording scan data and check whether the fluctuation starts in engine speed before it shows in the pulley speeds.
mistakes.detect: If the engine speed trace wobbles first and the pulley speeds follow it, the cause is upstream of the CVT.

mistakes.title: Blaming harsh engagement on clutches
mistakes.what: Treats hard garage shifts as worn clutches without first clearing up stored codes and comparing commanded with actual secondary pressure.
mistakes.consequence: Most sensor and solenoid faults make the TCM command maximum secondary pressure, so an overhaul leaves the real fault in place.
mistakes.prevent: Fix every stored code first, compare commanded and actual secondary pressure, and run the pressure learning procedures before condemning hard parts.

mistakes.title: Not noting fluid temperature with faults
mistakes.what: Records a lock-up or solenoid complaint without noting the CVTF temperature at the moment it happens.
mistakes.consequence: Heat-dependent faults, such as a lock-up solenoid that only opens when hot, look intermittent and pass a cold bench check.
mistakes.prevent: Write down the CVTF temperature for every check and try to reproduce the fault both cold and fully hot before teardown.

steps.title: Drain and inspect the fluid
steps.action: Pull the pan drain plug, catch the CVTF in a clean pan and look at it: metal glitter, a varnish smell or a milky look each point to a different failure.
steps.why: The drained fluid is your first look inside; debris here is what usually condemns the chain and pulleys.

mistakes.title: Ignoring burnt or metal-laden fluid
mistakes.what: Finds burnt-smelling or heavily contaminated CVTF but still plans a light repair such as a valve body swap or a reseal.
mistakes.consequence: Debris has already passed through the converter, cooler, valve body and pulleys, so the light repair fails again within a short time.
mistakes.prevent: Let the fluid set the scope: Subaru sends burnt or contaminated fluid to unit replacement and allows part repairs only on clean fluid.

mistakes.title: Opening the wrong drain plug
mistakes.what: Pulls the front differential drain plug thinking it is the CVT drain, or the reverse.
mistakes.consequence: Gear oil is judged as CVTF and the wrong failure is assumed; on a serviced car one unit is left empty and the other overfilled.
mistakes.prevent: Identify the CVT pan drain and the differential drain before loosening either, and confirm what comes out looks and smells like CVTF.

mistakes.title: Catching fluid in a dirty pan
mistakes.what: Drains the CVT into a pan that still holds old oil, sludge or metal from another job.
mistakes.consequence: You can no longer tell which glitter, colour or smell came from this CVT, so the drained fluid tells you nothing reliable.
mistakes.prevent: Drain into a clean pan, then pour a sample over a white rag and check the drain magnet before anything else touches it.

steps.title: Drain the front differential
steps.action: Drain the front differential gear oil separately from the CVTF and check the plug magnet for gear debris.
steps.why: On this unit the final drive has its own gear oil, so it is drained and judged on its own.

mistakes.title: Skipping the differential magnet check
mistakes.what: Drains the gear oil and throws it out without looking at the plug magnet and the oil for chips or paste.
mistakes.consequence: Worn hypoid gears or differential bearings go unnoticed, and the rebuilt CVT goes back in with a failing final drive.
mistakes.prevent: Look at the differential plug magnet and the drained gear oil before cleaning anything, and note chips separately from fine paste.

mistakes.title: Assuming one fluid fills both
mistakes.what: Treats the front differential as part of the CVT sump and drains only the CVT.
mistakes.consequence: The final drive is rebuilt around old gear oil, and at refill time one compartment is likely to get the other's fluid.
mistakes.prevent: Remember the front differential has its own 75W-90 GL-5 gear oil with its own drain and fill, and service it separately.

steps.title: Unbolt converter from drive plate
steps.action: Through the starter or access hole, rotate the engine and remove the converter-to-drive-plate nuts, then hold the converter back against the transmission.
steps.why: The converter must leave with the transmission; if it stays on the drive plate it drops off the pump drive and gets damaged.
steps.mistake: Letting the converter slide forward off its hub as the unit is separated, which damages the seal and pump drive.

mistakes.title: Converter slides off its hub
mistakes.what: Lets the converter ride forward with the drive plate as the CVT is separated from the engine.
mistakes.consequence: The converter drops off its hub, damaging the converter seal, the hub and the chain-driven oil pump drive.
mistakes.prevent: Once the nuts are out, push the converter fully back into the CVT and strap it to the housing before the unit moves.

mistakes.title: Separating with a nut still on
mistakes.what: Loses count while turning the engine and starts pulling the CVT back with one converter nut still fitted.
mistakes.consequence: The drive plate or a converter stud is bent or torn as the jack pulls the unit rearward.
mistakes.prevent: Count the converter nuts off against the number of studs and check the converter moves back from the plate by hand first.
mistakes.detect: The converter will not slide back from the drive plate.

steps.title: Lower the CVT out
steps.action: With the engine supported, disconnect the axles, propeller shaft, cooler lines, harness and crossmember, separate the CVT from the engine and lower it out on a jack.
steps.why: This is a summary of the in-car removal; the bench work starts once the unit is on the floor.

mistakes.title: Letting the CVT hang on dowels
mistakes.what: Removes the last bell housing bolts before the transmission jack is carrying the weight.
mistakes.consequence: The unit swings on the dowels and input shaft, bending the shaft, damaging the converter seal or cracking a housing ear.
mistakes.prevent: Take the full weight of the CVT on the jack and chain it to the saddle before the final housing bolts come out.

mistakes.title: Lowering with something still connected
mistakes.what: Lowers the CVT with a connector, ground strap or cooler line still attached.
mistakes.consequence: A harness connector is torn or a cooler pipe kinked, and it has to be replaced before the car can go back together.
mistakes.prevent: Walk around the unit with a light and check every connector, ground strap and line is free before the jack comes down.

mistakes.title: Leaving cooler lines open
mistakes.what: Leaves the disconnected cooler lines and CVT cooler ports uncapped while the car sits.
mistakes.consequence: Dirt gets into the cooler circuit and is later pumped straight into the rebuilt unit on first start.
mistakes.prevent: Cap both cooler lines and both ports as soon as they are disconnected, and still flush the cooler before reconnecting.

steps.title: Mount and clean the unit
steps.action: Stand the CVT securely on a bench fixture, then degrease the outside, especially the chain cover seam and bell housing, before any cover comes off.

mistakes.title: Opening covers before degreasing
mistakes.what: Removes a cover, plug or sensor before the outside of the unit is cleaned.
mistakes.consequence: Road grit packed around the seams falls into the valve body and case and ends up in valves and bearings.
mistakes.prevent: Degrease and dry the whole outside, especially the chain cover seam and bell housing, before any fastener is turned.

mistakes.title: Working the unit unsecured
mistakes.what: Sets the CVT on a bench or the floor without bolting it to a fixture.
mistakes.consequence: The unit tips when the case bolts or the pulley expander are worked, dropping parts or cracking the case.
mistakes.prevent: Bolt the CVT to a stand that holds it steady in each position the teardown needs, bell housing down for the case split.

steps.why: Road dirt around the seams falls straight into the hydraulics once covers are off.

steps.title: Slide out the torque converter
steps.action: Pull the converter straight forward off the input shaft with steady even pressure, letting the residual fluid drain into a pan.

mistakes.title: Pulling the converter at an angle
mistakes.what: Rocks or cocks the converter as it comes off the input shaft.
mistakes.consequence: The converter hub scores the stator support and seal surfaces or levers on the pump drive.
mistakes.prevent: Pull the converter straight forward with even pressure from both sides, using converter handles rather than fingers.

mistakes.title: Dropping the converter
mistakes.what: Lets the fluid-slick converter slide off the shaft unsupported.
mistakes.consequence: A dented shell or damaged hub means the converter can no longer be reused or economically rebuilt.
mistakes.prevent: Support the converter's weight with both hands as the hub clears the shaft, working over a drain pan.

mistakes.title: Not looking at converter fluid
mistakes.what: Lets the converter drain without looking at what comes out of it.
mistakes.consequence: Metal or friction debris inside the converter goes unnoticed, and that debris is the main evidence for replacing it.
mistakes.prevent: Drain the converter into a clean pan and look for metal and friction material before deciding whether it can stay.

steps.title: Check the chain cover seam
steps.action: Look around the oil pump chain cover and input shaft seal for wet, dirty CVTF trails and note them.
steps.why: Subaru names this cover's sealant and the input shaft seal as the usual CVTF seepage points on this unit.

mistakes.title: Assuming the leak is CVT fluid
mistakes.what: Sees a wet bell housing and assumes the chain cover is leaking without confirming the fluid is CVTF.
mistakes.consequence: An engine oil leak is left in place, and the resealed CVT comes back looking like it still leaks.
mistakes.prevent: Confirm the wet fluid is CVTF and not engine oil before choosing the repair, as Subaru's seepage bulletin requires first.

mistakes.title: Misreading fresh fluid at the seal
mistakes.what: Treats the small amount of fresh CVTF that appears at the bottom of the seal when the converter comes out as the leak.
mistakes.consequence: The real seepage path, old dirty trails at the cover seam or input seal, never gets recorded or repaired.
mistakes.prevent: Look for road dirt mixed with CVTF around the chain cover seam rather than clean fresh fluid at the bottom of the seal.

steps.title: Remove the top valve cover
steps.action: Take out the bolts around the cover on top of the case, lift it off and unplug the main connector, noting how each solenoid lead and ground is routed.
steps.why: On the TR580 the valve body sits on top of the case, and misrouted solenoid grounds set codes after the rebuild.

mistakes.title: Lifting the cover with harness attached
mistakes.what: Pulls the top cover off without first unplugging the valve body harness connector underneath it.
mistakes.consequence: The harness or its connector is torn, which turns a cover removal into a harness or valve body replacement.
mistakes.prevent: Lift the top cover only far enough to reach the connector, unplug it, then lift the cover clear.

mistakes.title: Not recording lead and ground routing
mistakes.what: Unplugs and moves solenoid leads without photographing their routing and ground points.
mistakes.consequence: Leads end up pinched under the cover or a ground is left loose, setting solenoid circuit codes after the rebuild.
mistakes.prevent: Photograph every solenoid lead and ground before touching them and label anything that could fit two places.

steps.title: Lift out the control valve body
steps.action: Remove the valve body to case bolts and lift it off level, then find the two small O-rings that can stay behind in the case.
steps.why: Lifting it level keeps loose valve parts in place, and the O-rings are easy to lose.
steps.mistake: Leaving the two case O-rings in their bores and later stacking new ones on top of them.

mistakes.title: Old case O-rings left behind
mistakes.what: Lifts the valve body without accounting for the two small O-rings that can stay in the case or stick to the valve body.
mistakes.consequence: The old rings are missed and new ones get stacked on top, which holds the valve body off the case and lets pressure leak.
mistakes.prevent: Count both valve body O-rings out at removal and bag them, then check the case bores are empty before new ones go in.

mistakes.title: Removing the valve body's own bolts
mistakes.what: Takes out bolts that hold the valve body sections together instead of only the nine body-to-case bolts.
mistakes.consequence: The body separates and its small filters, relief valves and springs drop into the case or get lost.
mistakes.prevent: Identify the nine 10 mm body-to-case bolts before turning anything and leave every other valve body bolt alone.
mistakes.detect: The valve body sections shift or a part falls out as it is lifted.

mistakes.title: Tipping the valve body over
mistakes.what: Lifts the valve body at an angle or turns it over to look underneath.
mistakes.consequence: Loose valves, filters and springs fall out of their bores and their positions are no longer known.
mistakes.prevent: Lift the valve body level and set it right side up on a clean tray until it is inspected.

mistakes.title: Mixing valve body bolts with others
mistakes.what: Drops the valve body bolts into the same tray as cover, pan and pump bolts.
mistakes.consequence: A bolt of the wrong length bottoms out in, or pulls threads from, the aluminum when it goes back in.
mistakes.prevent: Bag and label each group of bolts by location and compare lengths before reinstalling any of them.

steps.title: Remove the extension case
steps.action: Remove the extension case bolts, work the housing off the rear of the case and save the small O-ring that seals the transfer clutch feed.

mistakes.title: Losing the transfer clutch O-ring
mistakes.what: Pulls the extension case and lets the small O-ring that seals the transfer clutch feed fall out or stay stuck unnoticed.
mistakes.consequence: If it is missed on reassembly, the AWD transfer clutch gets little or no apply pressure.
mistakes.prevent: Find the transfer clutch feed O-ring and bag it as soon as the extension case is off.

mistakes.title: Prying the extension case seam
mistakes.what: Drives a screwdriver into the joint between the extension case and the main case.
mistakes.consequence: A gouged aluminum face leaks at the tail housing joint afterward and may need a new housing.
mistakes.prevent: Break the extension case joint with a soft mallet or at cast pry points, never on the machined faces.

steps.why: Without that O-ring the AWD clutch loses apply pressure.

steps.title: Bag and label transfer shims
steps.action: Collect the transfer gear shims as they come off and keep each set with its location; the two sets have different outside diameters.
steps.why: These shims set transfer gear bearing preload and end play; reusing them in the right place saves a full measurement.
steps.mistake: Mixing the two shim sets or losing one stuck to the housing.

mistakes.title: Mixing up the transfer shim sets
mistakes.what: Puts both transfer shim sets in one bag, or leaves one stuck to the housing.
mistakes.consequence: Transfer gear bearing preload and end play come out wrong, giving noise and early bearing failure or a second teardown.
mistakes.prevent: Bag each transfer shim set the moment it comes off, label its location, and check the housing bore for a stuck shim.
mistakes.detect: The two sets have different outside diameters, so a shim that doesn't fit its bore is in the wrong place.

mistakes.title: Bending a shim on removal
mistakes.what: Pries transfer shims off with a screwdriver tip.
mistakes.consequence: A bent shim no longer has its marked thickness, so preload changes even when it goes back in the right place.
mistakes.prevent: Lift shims with a thin pick or magnet, check each with a micrometer, and replace any that are bent or creased.

steps.title: Remove the parking pawl
steps.action: Take out the parking pawl with its spring and pivot shaft.

mistakes.title: Not noting the pawl spring hookup
mistakes.what: Removes the parking pawl, spring and shaft without noting how the spring hooks onto the pawl and case.
mistakes.consequence: Refitted wrong, the pawl may not retract and can ratchet against the park gear while driving, or Park may not hold.
mistakes.prevent: Photograph the pawl spring in place before removal so it can be hooked up exactly the same way.

steps.title: Pull transfer clutch drum and hub
steps.action: Pull the transfer clutch drum straight out of the rear of the case, then lift out the hub behind it.

mistakes.title: Letting the hub drop with drum
mistakes.what: Pulls the transfer clutch drum out with the hub still inside and lets the hub fall.
mistakes.consequence: The hub's sealing ring and ring lands are nicked, so the AWD clutch can leak apply pressure later.
mistakes.prevent: Pull the transfer drum straight out, then lift the hub out separately by hand.

mistakes.title: Stripping the pack before measuring
mistakes.what: Takes the transfer clutch apart without first checking its as-found clearance.
mistakes.consequence: You lose the clue that tells whether an AWD bind or slip complaint came from a tight or a worn pack.
mistakes.prevent: Measure the transfer pack clearance as found and write it down before the snap ring comes out.

steps.title: Remove transfer shaft and gears
steps.action: Take out the transfer shaft and its gears as an assembly.

mistakes.title: Levering the gears by their teeth
mistakes.what: Pries the transfer shaft and gears out using the gear teeth as a lever point.
mistakes.consequence: Chipped transfer gear teeth whine in service and leave metal in the CVTF.
mistakes.prevent: Lift the transfer assembly by its shaft and free it from the case side, never with a bar on a tooth.

steps.title: Remove the oil pan
steps.action: Unbolt and lift off the oil pan, then look at the magnet and the bottom of the pan for chain or pulley debris.

mistakes.title: Cleaning the pan before reading it
mistakes.what: Wipes the oil pan and magnet before looking at the debris.
mistakes.consequence: The evidence that separates chain and pulley wear, bearing failure and clutch wear is wiped away before anyone reads it.
mistakes.prevent: Photograph and examine the pan magnet and the bottom of the pan before any cleaning starts.

mistakes.title: Bending the pan flange
mistakes.what: Pries the oil pan off at one corner.
mistakes.consequence: A distorted pan flange will not sit flat again and leaks after reassembly.
mistakes.prevent: Cut the pan seal with a thin blade, and check the flange is flat on a surface before refitting.

steps.title: Remove strainer and pan baffle
steps.action: Remove the strainer bolts and pull the strainer, checking its O-ring, then unbolt the baffle under it from the case.

spec.note: each for the strainer and the baffle (baffle bolts 12 mm)

mistakes.title: Strainer O-ring left in the bore
mistakes.what: Pulls the strainer and leaves its O-ring stuck in the case bore.
mistakes.consequence: The new O-ring stacks on the old one or does not seat, the pump draws air, and the result is noise, low pressure and a risk of chain slip.
mistakes.prevent: Check the strainer bore is empty, with the old O-ring accounted for, before fitting the new strainer.

mistakes.title: Not looking inside the strainer
mistakes.what: Throws the old strainer away without looking at what it trapped.
mistakes.consequence: Large debris that points to a specific failed part, such as guide plastic or bearing chips, is missed.
mistakes.prevent: Look into the strainer inlet and shake it out over a clean pan before discarding it.

steps.title: Remove linkage and range switch
steps.action: Remove the manual valve linkage bolts, drive out the roll pin on the shift rail shaft and unbolt the inhibitor (range) switch.

mistakes.title: Not marking range switch position
mistakes.what: Unbolts the inhibitor switch without marking where it sat on the case.
mistakes.consequence: Refitted out of position, the car may not start in P or N, the reverse lamps misbehave and the TCM sees the wrong range.
mistakes.prevent: Scribe a line across the switch and case before removal, and still set the switch in neutral at reassembly.

mistakes.title: Damaging the shift rail roll pin
mistakes.what: Drives the roll pin out with an oversize or tapered punch, or without supporting the shaft.
mistakes.consequence: The pin mushrooms in its bore or the shift rail shaft bends, and the linkage gets sloppy.
mistakes.prevent: Use a pin punch of the right size, support the shaft behind the pin, and plan on a new roll pin.

steps.title: Remove the parking rod
steps.action: Pull the parking rod out before the case is touched.
steps.why: Left in place, the parking rod and manual valve linkage can bend when the main case is lifted off.
steps.mistake: Splitting the case with the parking rod still installed.

mistakes.title: Splitting the case with linkage in
mistakes.what: Starts lifting the main case while the parking rod and manual valve linkage are still installed.
mistakes.consequence: The rod or manual valve bends as the case rises, which means new parts and can leave Park or range selection faulty.
mistakes.prevent: Before touching any case bolt, confirm the parking rod and manual valve linkage are both out of the case.

steps.title: Remove the external sensors
steps.action: Remove the speed sensors and the secondary pressure sensor and cap the bores.

mistakes.title: Prying sensors out by the connector
mistakes.what: Levers the speed sensors or the secondary pressure sensor out by their plastic bodies or connectors.
mistakes.consequence: A cracked sensor or damaged connector sets speed sensor or P0841 codes after the rebuild.
mistakes.prevent: Twist each sensor gently to break its O-ring free and pull on the metal body only.

mistakes.title: Leaving sensor bores open
mistakes.what: Leaves the speed and pressure sensor bores uncapped for the rest of the teardown.
mistakes.consequence: Grit and cleaning solvent get into the case through the open sensor bores.
mistakes.prevent: Cap or tape every sensor bore as soon as its sensor is out.

steps.title: Pry off the chain cover
steps.action: Remove the pump chain cover bolts and pry the cover free only at its pry tabs, never on the machined face.
steps.why: A gouged sealing face is a guaranteed leak and may mean a new cover.

spec.note: 12 mm hex, all the same length on the TR580

steps.mistake: Prying on the machined sealing surface instead of the tabs.

mistakes.title: Prying on the machined face
mistakes.what: Puts the pry tool in the seam on the chain cover's sealing face instead of on its pry tabs.
mistakes.consequence: A gouged face leaks after reassembly, and Subaru's answer to a damaged face is a new cover.
mistakes.prevent: Pry only on the tabs Subaru shows, and keep prying only on them even after the cover breaks loose.
mistakes.detect: Run a fingernail around both faces after removal; any catch is damage.

mistakes.title: Prying with a bolt still in
mistakes.what: Starts prying the chain cover before all ten bolts are out.
mistakes.consequence: The chain cover cracks at a bolt boss and has to be replaced along with its seal.
mistakes.prevent: Count all ten 12 mm chain cover bolts out onto the bench before any prying starts.

steps.title: Remove the pump drive chain
steps.action: Lift off the oil pump drive chain and its sprockets together.
steps.why: The pump is chain-driven from the converter at about 1.33 times engine speed.

mistakes.title: Not marking the pump chain
mistakes.what: Lifts the oil pump drive chain off without marking which side faced out.
mistakes.consequence: A reused pump chain can go back flipped, putting its worn faces against fresh sprocket teeth.
mistakes.prevent: Paint-mark the outer face of the pump chain before removal, or replace it if it shows wear.

steps.title: Unbolt the oil pump
steps.action: Remove the pump bolts and lift the pump off, noting the large suction-side O-ring and the small pressure-side O-ring.

mistakes.title: Losing track of pump O-rings
mistakes.what: Lifts the oil pump and loses track of which O-ring sealed the suction port and which the output.
mistakes.consequence: Swapped or missing O-rings let the pump suck air or leak pressure, giving low line pressure and noise.
mistakes.prevent: Note that the large O-ring seals the suction side and the small one the output, and replace both with new rings.

mistakes.title: Rounding the 8 mm Allen bolts
mistakes.what: Uses a worn hex bit that is not fully seated in the pump bolt heads.
mistakes.consequence: A rounded pump bolt head has to be drilled or extracted from the case.
mistakes.prevent: Use a sharp 8 mm hex bit, seat it fully and keep the breaker bar square to the bolt.

steps.title: Remove the case-half bolts
steps.action: Remove every bolt joining the transmission case to the converter case, checking for any hidden in recesses.

mistakes.title: Missing a hidden case bolt
mistakes.what: Overlooks a case bolt in a recess and starts prying the case halves apart.
mistakes.consequence: The case flange or a bolt ear cracks, and a new case also means re-measuring shims.
mistakes.prevent: Count the case bolts out with a light, and expect the case to lift with only light prying at the lugs.

mistakes.title: Mixing case bolt lengths
mistakes.what: Throws all the case-half bolts into one tray.
mistakes.consequence: A long bolt in a short hole bottoms out or strips the aluminum thread in the converter case.
mistakes.prevent: Push each case bolt through a cardboard outline of the case in the position it came from.

steps.title: Lift off the transmission case
steps.action: Break the sealant and lift the transmission case straight off the converter case, leaving the variator standing.

mistakes.title: Missing the case passage O-rings
mistakes.what: Lifts the case without catching the two O-rings on its back that seal case passages.
mistakes.consequence: If they are lost or left out later, a hydraulic circuit leaks inside the unit and the case has to come off again.
mistakes.prevent: Find and bag both case passage O-rings as soon as the transmission case is off.

mistakes.title: Lifting the case crooked
mistakes.what: Tilts the transmission case as it rises off the pulley shafts.
mistakes.consequence: The case drags on the pulley bearings or knocks the chain and guides on its way up.
mistakes.prevent: Lift the case straight up, with a helper or hoist on a heavy unit, keeping it level the whole way.

mistakes.title: Chiseling the case seam
mistakes.what: Drives a chisel or screwdriver into the case joint to break the sealant.
mistakes.consequence: The gouged mating faces leak at the case seam once the unit is back in service.
mistakes.prevent: Break the case seal with a soft mallet or at the cast pry points only.

steps.title: Remove the secondary pulley baffle
steps.action: Unbolt and remove the baffle wrapped around the secondary pulley.

mistakes.title: Bending the pulley baffle
mistakes.what: Levers the baffle off around the secondary pulley before all three bolts are out.
mistakes.consequence: A bent baffle rubs the secondary pulley or chain once running, making noise and debris.
mistakes.prevent: Remove all three baffle bolts, lift it straight off, and check its shape before reuse.

steps.title: Open the secondary pulley
steps.action: Fit the pulley expander tool and tighten it evenly on both sides until the secondary pulley opens and the chain goes slack.
steps.why: The chain cannot come off a loaded pulley, and the secondary pulley is held closed by a strong spring.
tools: Secondary pulley expander tool (factory tool is discontinued; shops fabricate a plate and all-thread tool)
steps.mistake: Tightening one side of the tool ahead of the other so the pulley cocks or the tool slips under spring load.

mistakes.title: Tightening the expander unevenly
mistakes.what: Runs one side of the all-thread expander ahead of the other.
mistakes.consequence: The secondary pulley cocks, or the tool slips under spring load and the sheave slams shut.
mistakes.prevent: Alternate small turns side to side and check the sheave gap is the same on both sides as it opens.

mistakes.title: Using a flimsy homemade expander
mistakes.what: Builds the expander from thin plate or soft threaded rod.
mistakes.consequence: The plate bends or the threads strip under the strong spring, releasing the sheave suddenly onto the chain.
mistakes.prevent: Make the expander from stout plate and hardened threaded rod and check it for bending before every use.

mistakes.title: Tool bearing on a sheave face
mistakes.what: Lets the expander press on the working surface the chain runs on.
mistakes.consequence: The hardened face is dented or marked, and that mark then chews the chain.
mistakes.prevent: Pad every expander contact point and keep the tool well clear of the chain path on both sheaves.

steps.title: Release the chain guides
steps.action: Pull the chain outward, release the locking tabs and split the left chain guide, then remove its anchor bolt.

mistakes.title: Snapping the guide locking tabs
mistakes.what: Forces the plastic locking tabs on the chain guide.
mistakes.consequence: A guide with a broken tab can come apart in service, letting the chain wear into the oil supply tubes and drop pressure.
mistakes.prevent: Release the guide tabs one at a time with gentle pressure, and plan on new guides if any tab breaks.

mistakes.title: Splitting the guide before the anchor bolt
mistakes.what: Tries to work the left chain guide apart while its anchor bolt is still in.
mistakes.consequence: The guide cracks at the anchor, and a cracked guide cannot be reused.
mistakes.prevent: Remove the guide anchor bolt as part of releasing the guide, before any force goes on it.

steps.title: Unbolt the primary pulley
steps.action: Remove the bolts that retain the primary pulley on the right side.

mistakes.title: Mixing primary and secondary bolts
mistakes.what: Puts the primary pulley retaining bolts in with the secondary pulley bolts.
mistakes.consequence: A wrong-length bolt bottoms out or under-clamps the bearing retainer when the pulley goes back in.
mistakes.prevent: Bag the retaining bolts for each pulley separately and label the bags primary and secondary.

steps.title: Tip out the primary pulley
steps.action: Lift the primary pulley and tip it toward the secondary, take out the right chain guide, then remove the primary pulley and chain.
steps.why: Tipping the pulley in is the only way to gain room for the second guide.
steps.mistake: Letting the chain drop or the sheave faces knock together, which nicks the hardened surfaces.

mistakes.title: Knocking the sheave faces together
mistakes.what: Lets the chain drop or the primary sheave faces strike the secondary pulley or case as the pulley tips.
mistakes.consequence: Nicks in the hardened faces chew a chain, so the pulley has to be replaced.
mistakes.prevent: Tip the primary slowly with a helper holding the chain, and pad the secondary sheave with a clean lint-free cloth.

mistakes.title: Lifting the primary straight up
mistakes.what: Tries to pull the primary pulley straight out without tipping it toward the secondary.
mistakes.consequence: The pulley binds against the pinion shaft and the right guide or the pulley gets damaged.
mistakes.prevent: Tip the primary pulley toward the secondary to gain room for the right guide, as the step describes.

mistakes.title: Forcing out the right guide
mistakes.what: Pries the right chain guide past the pinion shaft before the pulley is tipped far enough.
mistakes.consequence: The right guide breaks against the pinion shaft and must be replaced.
mistakes.prevent: Tip the primary further until the right guide lifts out with no force at all.

steps.title: Mark and store the chain
steps.action: Mark the chain's running direction and lay it flat and clean where nothing can kink or nick it.
steps.why: If the chain is judged reusable it must go back the same way it wore in.

mistakes.title: Not marking chain running direction
mistakes.what: Removes the variator chain without marking which way it ran.
mistakes.consequence: If the chain is reused, it can go back the opposite way to how it wore in.
mistakes.prevent: Paint an arrow on an outer link plate before removal; never scribe or punch the chain.

mistakes.title: Storing the chain dirty or kinked
mistakes.what: Coils the variator chain tightly or lays it on a dirty bench.
mistakes.consequence: Grit lodges between the pins and plates, or a link is kinked, and a usable chain becomes scrap.
mistakes.prevent: Lay the chain flat in a clean covered tray away from the work until it is inspected.

steps.title: Remove the secondary pulley
steps.action: Back off the expander tool, remove the secondary pulley retaining bolts and lift the pulley out, keeping the shims from its rear.
steps.mistake: Losing the rear pulley shims, which set the pulley's axial position.

mistakes.title: Losing the rear pulley shims
mistakes.what: Lifts the secondary pulley out and lets the shims behind it fall or stay stuck unseen.
mistakes.consequence: The pulley ends up in the wrong axial position, so the chain runs misaligned and wears both pulleys.
mistakes.prevent: Bag and label the secondary rear shims as the pulley comes out and measure them with a micrometer.

mistakes.title: Releasing the expander too fast
mistakes.what: Spins the expander nuts off quickly to save time once the chain is out.
mistakes.consequence: The sheave snaps shut under spring force, which can damage the sheave, its seals or the tool.
mistakes.prevent: Back the expander off evenly in small turns on each side until the spring is fully unloaded.

steps.title: Collect the primary pulley shim
steps.action: Recover the shim from the primary pulley front bearing and tag it with its location.
steps.why: Pulley shims set where each pulley sits; a wrong stack misaligns the chain.

mistakes.title: Primary shim not tagged
mistakes.what: Drops the primary front bearing shim in with the secondary rear shims.
mistakes.consequence: Swapped shims move both pulleys out of line and misalign the chain.
mistakes.prevent: Bag the primary front bearing shim on its own and label it with its location.

steps.title: Remove the internal manual valve
steps.action: Unbolt the manual valve body and separator plate from the reverse brake housing.

mistakes.title: Separator plate orientation lost
mistakes.what: Lets the separator plate come away from the internal manual valve body without marking which face goes where.
mistakes.consequence: Refitted flipped, its holes no longer match the passages and forward or reverse feed is blocked.
mistakes.prevent: Mark the separator plate face before it is separated and keep it with its own valve body.

steps.title: Remove the reverse brake
steps.action: Remove the housing support bolts, then lift out the reverse brake plates in order, noting which way the dished cushion plate faces.

mistakes.title: Not noting the cushion plate direction
mistakes.what: Lifts out the reverse plates without noting which way the dished cushion plate faces.
mistakes.consequence: Refitted backward, reverse engagement is harsh or erratic and the clearance reading is wrong.
mistakes.prevent: Note the cushion plate's ID mark, which faces the assembler, and keep the plates in order.

mistakes.title: Mixing reverse and forward plates
mistakes.what: Puts reverse brake plates in the same tray as forward clutch plates.
mistakes.consequence: The packs get the wrong counts, four and four in reverse against three and three in forward, and clearance can't be set.
mistakes.prevent: Use separate labelled trays for the reverse brake and the forward clutch plates.

mistakes.title: Rounding the E20 bolt heads
mistakes.what: Uses a hex or worn socket on the reverse brake housing support bolts.
mistakes.consequence: Damaged Torx heads have to be cut or extracted from the housing.
mistakes.prevent: Use a proper E20 Torx socket, seated fully, on the housing support bolts.

steps.title: Remove the planetary gear set
steps.action: Lift out the ring gear, planet carrier and sun gear, noting which way the sun gear faces.

mistakes.title: Not noting sun gear direction
mistakes.what: Lifts the sun gear out without noting which side the full-circle oil slot faced.
mistakes.consequence: On reassembly it can go in backward and starve the planetary of lube oil.
mistakes.prevent: Note the slot pattern at removal: full-circle slot toward the drum, three-slot side toward the planet.

steps.title: Remove the forward drum
steps.action: Remove the forward clutch drum together with the input shaft, then take out the snap ring and the forward clutch plates in order.
steps.why: On the TR580 the forward clutch rides on the input shaft ahead of the primary pulley.

mistakes.title: Nicking the input shaft ring lands
mistakes.what: Handles or rests the input shaft on its sealing ring area.
mistakes.consequence: Nicked lands or grooves leak forward clutch apply oil even with new sealing rings.
mistakes.prevent: Hold the input shaft by its ends and set it down on a padded cradle.

mistakes.title: Dumping the clutch plates together
mistakes.what: Pulls the forward clutch plates out in a pile.
mistakes.consequence: You can no longer read the wear pattern plate by plate, and the cushion plate direction is lost.
mistakes.prevent: Lay the forward clutch plates out in removal order on a clean towel.

steps.title: Lift out the pinion support
steps.action: Remove the pinion support bolts and pry the support up with the drive pinion, saving the two seals.

mistakes.title: Prying the pinion support on its bore
mistakes.what: Levers the pinion support up against the case sealing bore.
mistakes.consequence: A gouged bore leaks past the new support seals, and the case may have to be replaced.
mistakes.prevent: Pry the pinion support only at its pry points, evenly from both sides.

mistakes.title: Losing track of the support seals
mistakes.what: Discards the two pinion support seals without noting where each sat.
mistakes.consequence: The new seals can go into the wrong grooves on the support and leak.
mistakes.prevent: Note each pinion support seal's position and compare the new ones with the old before fitting.

steps.title: Lift out the front differential
steps.action: Lift the front differential out of the converter case.

mistakes.title: Knocking the hypoid gear teeth
mistakes.what: Lets the ring gear teeth strike the case as the differential is lifted out.
mistakes.consequence: Chipped hypoid teeth whine and shed metal into the differential gear oil.
mistakes.prevent: Lift the differential straight out by its case, guiding the ring gear clear of the housing.

steps.title: Drive out the old seals
steps.action: Remove the converter seal, the stator and input shaft seals and both differential side seals.
steps.why: Subaru treats the axle side seals as one-time-use, and the input shaft seal was redesigned.

mistakes.title: Missing the stator shaft seal
mistakes.what: Removes the converter and input seals but overlooks the third seal at the base of the stator shaft.
mistakes.consequence: The old seal stays in, converter apply oil leaks, and lock-up becomes weak or shudders.
mistakes.prevent: Count all three front seals out, including the one that seals inside the converter hub.

mistakes.title: Gouging the seal bores
mistakes.what: Drives a chisel or screwdriver between the old seal and its bore.
mistakes.consequence: A scratched seal bore leaks around the outside of the new seal.
mistakes.prevent: Use a seal puller, or lever against the seal casing only, keeping metal off the bore.

mistakes.title: Keeping the axle side seals
mistakes.what: Leaves the original differential side seals in because they are not leaking.
mistakes.consequence: Subaru treats them as one-time-use, and the old seals are a likely leak once the axles are refitted.
mistakes.prevent: Replace both differential side seals as part of every CVT removal.

steps.title: Clean the cases and passages
steps.action: Wash every case and flush the passages, picking sealant crumbs out of the stator support cavity with tape, then check both chain cover sealing faces for nicks.
steps.why: Subaru says not to use abrasive pads or compressed air there, and a damaged face means a new cover.
steps.mistake: Using a gasket disc on the aluminum sealing faces.

mistakes.title: Gasket disc on the sealing faces
mistakes.what: Cleans the chain cover or case faces with an abrasive pad or gasket removal disc.
mistakes.consequence: The abraded aluminum no longer seals, and abrasive grit gets into passages and the pump.
mistakes.prevent: Clean the sealing faces with a plastic scraper and solvent only, as Subaru specifies.

mistakes.title: Blowing out the stator cavity
mistakes.what: Uses compressed air to clear sealant crumbs from around the stator support.
mistakes.consequence: The crumbs are blown deeper into passages, where they can block oil flow.
mistakes.prevent: Pick loose sealant out of the stator cavity with the sticky side of tape, as Subaru describes.

mistakes.title: Lint left in passages
mistakes.what: Wipes passages with shop rags and leaves lint and solvent behind.
mistakes.consequence: Lint clogs the small filters in the valve body and sticks valves in their bores.
mistakes.prevent: Use lint-free wipes, finish with a rinse of clean fluid, and let the cleaned parts dry covered.

mistakes.title: Not inspecting the cleaned faces
mistakes.what: Cleans the chain cover and case faces but does not inspect them closely.
mistakes.consequence: An existing nick or irregularity on a sealing face leaks after reassembly.
mistakes.prevent: Inspect both faces under good light, and if the cover is replaced confirm it carries the new-style input seal.

steps.title: Inspect the variator chain
steps.action: Check every link and pin for cracks, flat spots, heat colour and stretch, look for chipped plates, and check both plastic guides for grooves and broken tabs.
steps.why: Chain wear and broken guides are the usual sources of driving noise on this unit.

mistakes.title: Passing a chain by eye
mistakes.what: Looks at the outside of the variator chain and calls it good.
mistakes.consequence: Pin wear, cracked or chipped plates and heat damage go unseen, and the chain slips or fails later and takes the pulleys with it.
mistakes.prevent: Flex and inspect every link on both edges, look for heat colour and chipped plates, and judge stretch against a known reference.

mistakes.title: Reusing worn chain guides
mistakes.what: Puts back plastic chain guides with grooves, cracks or broken clips.
mistakes.consequence: A failing guide lets the chain rub the oil supply tubes, wearing them and dropping oil pressure.
mistakes.prevent: Replace guides that show grooves, cracks or damaged clips, and check the oil tubes for rub marks.

steps.title: Inspect the pulley sheave faces
steps.action: Look at all four sheave faces for scoring, steps, galling or bluing where the chain runs.
steps.why: Once the chain slips, chain and pulleys are damaged together.
steps.mistake: Fitting a new chain to scored pulleys, which destroys the new chain quickly.

mistakes.title: New chain on scored pulleys
mistakes.what: Fits a new chain to sheaves that show scoring or steps.
mistakes.consequence: The damaged faces wear the new chain quickly, slip returns, and the whole variator is lost.
mistakes.prevent: Replace chain and pulleys as a set whenever any of the four sheave faces is scored or stepped.

mistakes.title: Dressing scored sheave faces
mistakes.what: Tries to polish out sheave scoring with abrasive.
mistakes.consequence: The dressed face no longer matches the chain's contact, slip and wear return, and abrasive grit ends up in the hydraulics.
mistakes.prevent: Treat any sheave damage as a replacement decision; never put abrasive on a pulley face.

mistakes.title: Inspecting sheaves in poor light
mistakes.what: Checks the four sheave faces quickly under ordinary shop lighting.
mistakes.consequence: Fine steps, early galling and light bluing are missed and a damaged pulley is reused.
mistakes.prevent: Clean each sheave and inspect it under a strong light, feeling across the chain track with a fingernail.

steps.title: Decide reuse or replace variator
steps.action: Treat chain and pulleys as one decision: if either is damaged, replace the variator parts as a set or switch to a complete replacement CVT.
steps.why: Subaru's own fix for confirmed chain slip is a complete CVT, and loose pulleys and chains are hard to source.

mistakes.title: Not finding why the chain slipped
mistakes.what: Replaces chain and pulleys without finding the loss of secondary pressure that let the chain slip.
mistakes.consequence: A worn lube valve bore, a low fluid level or a pressure fault is still there and slips the new variator.
mistakes.prevent: Treat slip as a symptom: check secondary pressure control, valve body bores and fluid level in the same job.

mistakes.title: Mixing used variator parts
mistakes.what: Pairs a used pulley from another unit with this unit's chain or other pulley.
mistakes.consequence: Mismatched wear surfaces bring noise and slip, and the pulley shims no longer suit the parts.
mistakes.prevent: Keep chain and pulleys as one decision and go to a complete unit when matched variator parts can't be had.

steps.title: Check the pulley bearings
steps.action: Spin each pulley bearing for roughness and check the pulley sealing rings and grooves.

mistakes.title: Accepting a slightly rough bearing
mistakes.what: Puts a pulley back with a shaft bearing that feels a little rough.
mistakes.consequence: The bearing whines, then fails and sheds metal through the whole unit.
mistakes.prevent: Replace any pulley bearing that does not turn perfectly smooth by hand.

mistakes.title: Ignoring worn ring grooves
mistakes.what: Checks the pulley sealing rings but not the sides of their grooves.
mistakes.consequence: New rings leak in stepped grooves, the pulley loses clamping pressure and the chain slips.
mistakes.prevent: Inspect the pulley ring groove sides for steps and replace the part if they are worn.

mistakes.title: Spinning dry bearings with air
mistakes.what: Spins a cleaned pulley bearing with compressed air.
mistakes.consequence: The dry overspeed damages the bearing's balls and races and can throw it apart.
mistakes.prevent: Turn bearings slowly by hand with a little clean CVTF on them.

steps.title: Inspect clutch plates and pistons
steps.action: Check all three packs: frictions for burning and lost material, steels for heat spots and warping, and pistons, seals, return springs and drum bores for scoring.

mistakes.title: Reusing heat-marked steels
mistakes.what: Reuses steel clutch plates with blue heat spots or warping.
mistakes.consequence: New frictions glaze against the damaged steels, causing shudder and slip.
mistakes.prevent: Check each steel for flatness and heat marks and replace any that fail either check.

mistakes.title: Not checking piston bores
mistakes.what: Fits new piston seals without inspecting the drum and piston bores for scoring.
mistakes.consequence: New seals leak past a scored bore, giving slow apply and slip.
mistakes.prevent: Inspect every clutch piston bore and replace a scored drum or piston.

mistakes.title: Not finding why a pack burned
mistakes.what: Replaces burnt frictions without looking for the low apply pressure that burned them.
mistakes.consequence: A worn forward and reverse regulating valve bore keeps clutch pressure low, and the new pack burns again.
mistakes.prevent: Check the valve body's forward and reverse regulating valve bore for wear before closing up.

steps.title: Inspect the planetary gears
steps.action: Check the planet pinions for play and pitting, and the ring and sun gear teeth and oil slots.

mistakes.title: Passing worn planet pinions
mistakes.what: Spins the planet carrier once and calls it good.
mistakes.consequence: Worn pinion needles or pitted gears whine and shed debris later.
mistakes.prevent: Turn each planet pinion separately, checking for rough spots, end play and pitting.

mistakes.title: Missing blocked lube slots
mistakes.what: Doesn't check the sun and ring gear oil slots.
mistakes.consequence: A blocked slot starves the planetary of lube oil, and the pinions overheat.
mistakes.prevent: Clean every sun and ring gear oil slot and look through each one for a clear path.

steps.title: Split and inspect the pump
steps.action: Unbolt and separate the pump halves, check the gears, body, shaft and shaft bearings for wear and pitting, and check the pump drive chain and sprockets.

mistakes.title: Losing pump gear orientation
mistakes.what: Lifts the pump gears out without noting that their ID marks face into the pump body.
mistakes.consequence: Refitted upside down, the gears run on the wrong faces, losing pressure or scoring the pump.
mistakes.prevent: Note that the pump gear ID marks go into the body first, and recheck before the halves are closed.

mistakes.title: Reusing a scored pump
mistakes.what: Accepts scoring on the pump body or gear faces.
mistakes.consequence: Pump output falls, secondary pressure falls with it, and the chain can slip.
mistakes.prevent: Replace an oil pump whose body or gear faces are scored rather than hoping it holds pressure.

mistakes.title: Reusing a worn pump drive chain
mistakes.what: Reuses a pump drive chain or sprockets that show wear.
mistakes.consequence: Noise follows, and if the drive fails the pump stops and the CVT loses all pressure.
mistakes.prevent: Check the pump chain and sprocket teeth for wear and replace them as a set if worn.

spec.note: 10 mm heads hold the pump halves

steps.title: Decide on the torque converter
steps.action: Plan on a new, rebuilt or updated converter rather than reusing one from a debris failure, since it cannot be flushed clean.
steps.why: Subaru moved the converter from a thrust washer to a needle bearing after washer wear blocked lock-up release.

mistakes.title: Reusing a contaminated converter
mistakes.what: Flushes and reuses a converter after a debris failure.
mistakes.consequence: Debris trapped inside the converter washes into the new valve body and pulleys.
mistakes.prevent: Fit a new, remanufactured or properly rebuilt converter after any failure that put debris in the fluid.

mistakes.title: Fitting an early-design converter
mistakes.what: Installs an old-stock or used converter of the early thrust-washer design.
mistakes.consequence: Washer wear can block lock-up release, so the engine nearly stalls coming to a stop.
mistakes.prevent: Confirm the replacement converter is the updated design with a needle bearing in place of the washer.

mistakes.title: Blaming the converter for valve faults
mistakes.what: Replaces the converter for a lock-up complaint without testing the lock-up solenoid and TCC valve.
mistakes.consequence: A solenoid that opens when hot or a worn TCC boost valve bore gives the same symptoms, and the complaint returns.
mistakes.prevent: Test the lock-up solenoid hot and cold, check line pressure, and check the TCC valve bore before condemning the converter.

steps.title: Measure the solenoid resistances
steps.action: Measure each solenoid at room temperature, then recheck the lock-up solenoid hot, because it often opens only when warm.

spec.note: Lock-up duty, primary-up and primary-down. Secondary line pressure 5–7 Ω, forward/reverse 4–6 Ω, AWD 2.0–4.5 Ω (aftermarket figures)

mistakes.title: Checking the lock-up solenoid only cold
mistakes.what: Measures the lock-up duty solenoid at room temperature only.
mistakes.consequence: A solenoid that goes open circuit when hot passes the test, and the lock-up code returns once the car is warm.
mistakes.prevent: Heat the lock-up solenoid with a heat gun or oil bath while watching its resistance.
mistakes.detect: Resistance that jumps to open as it heats condemns the solenoid.

mistakes.title: Measuring through the harness only
mistakes.what: Reads resistances only at the main connector and judges the solenoids from that.
mistakes.consequence: Harness or connector resistance is mistaken for a solenoid fault, or a bad solenoid is hidden by the reading.
mistakes.prevent: Measure at each solenoid as well as through the harness, and compare the two readings.

mistakes.title: One resistance spec for all
mistakes.what: Applies the 10.0 to 13.5 ohm figure to every solenoid on the valve body.
mistakes.consequence: The secondary line pressure, forward/reverse and AWD solenoids read lower by design, so good parts are condemned.
mistakes.prevent: Check each of the six solenoids against its own resistance range, not the lock-up figure.

mistakes.title: Poor splice on a swapped solenoid
mistakes.what: Twists wires together or uses ordinary heat-shrink when fitting a lock-up solenoid from a core.
mistakes.consequence: The splice fails in hot fluid and the lock-up solenoid code returns.
mistakes.prevent: Solder the solenoid leads and cover the joint with oil-resistant heat-shrink only.

steps.title: Decide on the valve body
steps.action: Fit Subaru's updated valve body, or rebuild the worn bores with aftermarket valve and sleeve kits if you have the tooling.
steps.why: Subaru sells the valve body only as an assembly; the updated design fixes lock-up and shudder faults.

mistakes.title: Reusing a valve body with worn bores
mistakes.what: Refits the original valve body after a slip, burn or lock-up failure without checking its bores.
mistakes.consequence: A worn lube valve bore leaks secondary pressure and a worn forward and reverse regulating bore starves the clutches, so new parts fail.
mistakes.prevent: Fit Subaru's updated valve body, or ream the worn bores and fit oversize valve kits.

mistakes.title: Fitting a superseded valve body
mistakes.what: Installs a used or old-stock valve body of the earlier design.
mistakes.consequence: Lock-up codes or shudder can return, which is exactly what the updated part's enhanced valve sleeve was made to stop.
mistakes.prevent: Order the current Subaru valve body and confirm it is the updated design before fitting.

mistakes.title: Reaming bores without the fixture
mistakes.what: Attempts the oversize valve repair freehand.
mistakes.consequence: An off-axis or oversize bore makes the new valve stick and scraps the valve body.
mistakes.prevent: Use the kit maker's reamer set and holding fixture, or send the valve body to a shop that has them.

mistakes.title: Losing small filters and relief valves
mistakes.what: Separates the valve body without mapping the small filters and relief valves in its middle section.
mistakes.consequence: A part left out or in the wrong pocket changes a pressure circuit, bringing codes and harsh or slipping engagements.
mistakes.prevent: Photograph and map every small filter and relief valve as the separator plate comes off.

steps.title: Check the sensors and harness
steps.action: Check the speed sensor tips for debris, the pressure sensor connector, and the harness for chafing or oil in the connectors.

mistakes.title: Swapping the sensor on P0841 alone
mistakes.what: Replaces the secondary pressure sensor for P0841 without following the diagnostic flow.
mistakes.consequence: The code can come from wiring, loose terminals, contamination in a pressure solenoid or a hard-part failure, so it returns.
mistakes.prevent: Follow Subaru's P0841 flow, and check for a TCM reprogram that addresses solenoid contamination.

mistakes.title: Reusing a fluid-soaked connector
mistakes.what: Puts back a harness connector with CVTF inside it or loose terminals.
mistakes.consequence: Intermittent sensor or solenoid codes follow, and many of these faults default secondary pressure to maximum.
mistakes.prevent: Clean and dry the connector, inspect the pins, and check each terminal grips a test pin firmly.

mistakes.title: Ignoring debris on sensor tips
mistakes.what: Wipes metal off a speed sensor tip without asking where it came from.
mistakes.consequence: Metal on the tip distorts the speed signal, and whatever shed it is still inside the unit.
mistakes.prevent: Clean the sensor tip and trace the debris to its source before reassembly.

steps.title: Inspect the final drive
steps.action: Check the hypoid gear and drive pinion teeth, the side and pinion gears, and the differential and pinion bearings for pitting or roughness.

mistakes.title: Rebuilding around a worn differential
mistakes.what: Accepts pitted hypoid teeth or rough differential bearings.
mistakes.consequence: The final drive howls after the rebuild and the whole unit comes out again.
mistakes.prevent: Replace worn final drive parts now, and re-set pinion depth and backlash if they change.

steps.title: Inspect transfer gears and bearings
steps.action: Check the transfer gear teeth and bearings and the transfer clutch hub splines.

mistakes.title: Passing rough transfer gear bearings
mistakes.what: Reuses transfer gear bearings that feel rough because they are not in the kit.
mistakes.consequence: They whine, and replacing them later means removing the extension case and re-shimming.
mistakes.prevent: Spin each transfer bearing by hand, replace any that are rough, and re-measure the shims if they change.

mistakes.title: Ignoring worn transfer hub splines
mistakes.what: Overlooks stepped or worn splines on the transfer clutch hub.
mistakes.consequence: Plates hang up on the steps, so the AWD clutch drags or applies unevenly.
mistakes.prevent: Check the hub splines for steps where the plates ride and replace a worn hub.

steps.title: Replace the pulley shaft bearings
steps.action: Where a bearing is rough, unstake and remove the retaining nut, pull the bearing, press the new one on by its inner race, then restake the nut.
steps.why: Pressing on the outer race brinells a new bearing.
steps.mistake: Forgetting to restake the nut after torquing it.

mistakes.title: Not restaking the bearing nut
mistakes.what: Torques the pulley bearing retaining nut but doesn't stake it.
mistakes.consequence: The nut can back off, the bearing loosens and the pulley moves, wrecking the chain and pulleys.
mistakes.prevent: Stake the retaining nut after torquing it and check the stake has bitten into the shaft groove.

mistakes.title: Pressing through the outer race
mistakes.what: Presses the new pulley bearing on by its outer race.
mistakes.consequence: The load passes through the balls and brinells the new bearing, which then whines in service.
mistakes.prevent: Press the bearing on only by its inner race, using a driver sized to that race.

mistakes.title: Not rechecking pulley shims
mistakes.what: Fits new pulley bearings and reuses the old shim stack without checking.
mistakes.consequence: A bearing of slightly different width shifts the pulley's axial position and misaligns the chain.
mistakes.prevent: Re-measure pulley position and shim selection after any pulley bearing change.

steps.title: Fit new shaft sealing rings
steps.action: Fit new sealing rings on the pulley shafts and input shaft and lubricate them with CVTF.

mistakes.title: Cutting a sealing ring on install
mistakes.what: Stretches or drags a sealing ring over a sharp spline or groove edge.
mistakes.consequence: A damaged ring leaks pulley or clutch apply pressure, which can mean low clamping and chain slip.
mistakes.prevent: Use a ring installer or tape over the splines, and check each ring sits free and unbroken in its groove.

mistakes.title: Fitting sealing rings dry
mistakes.what: Installs the new shaft sealing rings without lubricating them.
mistakes.consequence: The rings can roll or be cut as each shaft enters its bore on assembly.
mistakes.prevent: Lubricate each shaft sealing ring with CVTF just before its shaft is installed.

steps.title: Reassemble the oil pump
steps.action: Lubricate the pump gears with CVTF, bolt the pump halves together and fit new O-rings on both ports.

mistakes.title: Pump gears upside down
mistakes.what: Installs the oil pump gears with their ID marks facing out.
mistakes.consequence: The gears run on the wrong faces against the pump body, losing pressure or scoring the pump.
mistakes.prevent: Fit the pump gears with the ID marks going into the body first, then check before closing.

mistakes.title: Assembling the pump dry
mistakes.what: Bolts the pump halves together without CVTF on the gears.
mistakes.consequence: The pump runs dry at first start and is slow to prime, scuffing its gears.
mistakes.prevent: Coat the pump gears and body pockets with CVTF before the halves go together.

mistakes.title: Not checking the pump turns
mistakes.what: Tightens the pump half bolts without checking the gears still turn.
mistakes.consequence: A pump that binds after its halves are pulled together scores its gears and loses output at idle.
mistakes.prevent: Tighten the four half bolts evenly in stages and turn the pump drive after each stage.

steps.title: Install the new input seal
steps.action: Press the redesigned input shaft seal into the chain cover until it is flush with the cover edge, oiling only the main lip.
steps.why: A seal driven too deep blocks the oil passage beside it.
steps.mistake: Driving the seal past flush and restricting the oil passage.

mistakes.title: Seal driven past flush
mistakes.what: Drives the new input seal deeper than flush with the chain cover edge.
mistakes.consequence: The seal restricts or blocks the oil passage beside it in the chain cover.
mistakes.prevent: Use the installer tool and stop with the seal flush to the chain cover edge, no deeper.
mistakes.detect: After fitting, the oil passage beside the seal should be fully clear.

mistakes.title: Fitting the old-style input seal
mistakes.what: Uses an old-style seal from stock or a kit that lacks the added side lip.
mistakes.consequence: Water and dust reach the main lip and the seepage the redesign fixes comes back, with the CVT out again to cure it.
mistakes.prevent: Confirm the input seal has the extra side lip before installing it.

mistakes.title: Driving the seal in cocked
mistakes.what: Taps the input seal in around its edge without an installer.
mistakes.consequence: A seal that sits crooked in its bore leaks around the input shaft.
mistakes.prevent: Use the seal installer so the input seal goes in square all the way round.

mistakes.title: Oiling more than the main lip
mistakes.what: Coats the whole input seal, including its outside and the side lip, with fluid.
mistakes.consequence: The seal can slip in its bore and the oily side lip collects road dirt.
mistakes.prevent: Put CVTF on the main lip only, as Subaru directs, and keep the outside dry.

steps.title: Rebuild the forward clutch
steps.action: Fit new piston seals, then stack the dished cushion plate with its ID mark facing you, soaked frictions alternating with steels, the pressure plate and snap ring.

spec.note: 3 steels, 1 pressure plate, 1 dished cushion plate

mistakes.title: Stacking frictions dry
mistakes.what: Builds the forward pack with new frictions straight out of the box.
mistakes.consequence: Dry frictions can scorch on the first engagements, and the clearance reading changes once they soak.
mistakes.prevent: Soak the forward frictions in CVTF before stacking and measure the pack with soaked plates.

mistakes.title: Cushion plate ID mark wrong
mistakes.what: Fits the forward dished cushion plate with its ID mark facing away.
mistakes.consequence: Drive engagement is harsh or erratic and the measured forward clearance is wrong.
mistakes.prevent: Fit the forward cushion plate with the ID mark facing you, as the teardown article shows.

mistakes.title: Rolling a piston seal
mistakes.what: Forces the forward piston into the drum and rolls or cuts a seal lip.
mistakes.consequence: Apply oil leaks past the forward piston, and the clutch slips and burns.
mistakes.prevent: Lubricate the piston seals, work the lip in with a smooth tool, and air-check the piston.

mistakes.title: Snap ring not fully seated
mistakes.what: Leaves the forward pack snap ring partly out of its groove.
mistakes.consequence: The pack can come apart under load and damage the forward drum.
mistakes.prevent: Check the snap ring all the way around and rotate it in its groove to confirm it is seated.

steps.title: Set forward clutch clearance
steps.action: Measure pack clearance with a feeler gauge and change the selective plate until it is in range.
steps.mistake: Accepting a loose pack, which slips and burns on engagement.

mistakes.title: Accepting a loose forward pack
mistakes.what: Leaves forward clutch clearance above range.
mistakes.consequence: Engagement into D is late and slips, and the forward pack burns.
mistakes.prevent: Change the forward selective apply plate until the clearance sits inside 1.10 to 1.40 mm.

mistakes.title: Building the forward pack tight
mistakes.what: Sets forward clutch clearance below range.
mistakes.consequence: The forward clutch drags when it should be released, heating the plates in neutral and reverse.
mistakes.prevent: Keep forward clearance inside the range; a tight pack is not a better pack.

mistakes.title: Measuring an unsettled pack
mistakes.what: Measures without pressing the plates down evenly, at one point only, or with dry frictions.
mistakes.consequence: The reading is off by enough that the wrong selective plate goes in.
mistakes.prevent: Settle the pack, measure at several points around it, and measure with soaked frictions.

mistakes.title: Using first-generation clearances
mistakes.what: Builds to clearances published for the 2010 to 2012 first-generation TR580.
mistakes.consequence: The Forester's second-generation unit has different packs, so the pack ends up outside its own range.
mistakes.prevent: Confirm the unit is the second generation and use the clearances published for it.

steps.title: Rebuild the reverse brake
steps.action: Fit new piston seals, then stack the dished cushion plate with its ID mark facing you, soaked frictions alternating with steels, then the pressure plate.

spec.note: 4 steels, 1 pressure plate, 1 dished cushion plate

mistakes.title: Reverse frictions not soaked
mistakes.what: Stacks new reverse brake frictions dry.
mistakes.consequence: They can scorch on the first reverse engagements, and the measured clearance changes once they soak.
mistakes.prevent: Soak the reverse frictions in CVTF first and measure the pack with soaked plates.

mistakes.title: Wrong reverse plate count
mistakes.what: Uses the forward pack's plate count or mixes plates between the packs.
mistakes.consequence: The reverse clearance can't be brought into range no matter which selective plate goes in.
mistakes.prevent: Stack four frictions and four steels with the cushion and pressure plates in the reverse brake.

mistakes.title: Reverse cushion plate reversed
mistakes.what: Fits the reverse cushion plate with its ID mark away from you.
mistakes.consequence: Reverse engagement is harsh and the reverse clearance reading is wrong.
mistakes.prevent: Fit the reverse cushion plate with its ID mark facing you before the frictions go in.

mistakes.title: Rolled reverse piston seal
mistakes.what: Rolls or cuts a reverse piston seal on assembly.
mistakes.consequence: Reverse applies late or slips under load, and the reverse pack burns.
mistakes.prevent: Lubricate the reverse piston seals, fit the piston gently and air-check it before stacking.

steps.title: Set reverse brake clearance
steps.action: Measure the reverse pack clearance and swap the selective plate until it falls in range.
steps.mistake: Building the pack tight, which drags in forward and overheats the plates.

mistakes.title: Building the reverse pack tight
mistakes.what: Sets reverse brake clearance below range.
mistakes.consequence: The reverse brake drags while driving forward, overheating its plates over every mile.
mistakes.prevent: Swap the selective plate until reverse clearance sits inside 2.30 to 2.70 mm.

mistakes.title: Leaving the reverse pack loose
mistakes.what: Accepts reverse brake clearance above range.
mistakes.consequence: Reverse engages late and harshly and the reverse pack wears quickly.
mistakes.prevent: Bring reverse clearance inside the range before the housing goes in.

mistakes.title: Trusting selective plate markings
mistakes.what: Picks a selective plate by its marking without measuring it.
mistakes.consequence: A mislabelled or worn plate puts the clearance out of range without anyone noticing.
mistakes.prevent: Measure each selective plate with a micrometer before choosing which one to fit.

steps.title: Stack the transfer clutch pack
steps.action: With a resealed piston, lay in the apply plate, then alternate steel and friction four times, then the pressure plate and snap ring.

spec.note: 4 steels, apply plate and pressure plate

mistakes.title: Apply plate in wrong position
mistakes.what: Starts the transfer stack with a friction instead of the apply plate.
mistakes.consequence: Transfer clearance and engagement are wrong, giving AWD bind or slip.
mistakes.prevent: Lay the apply plate in first, then alternate steel and friction four times.

mistakes.title: Transfer frictions stacked dry
mistakes.what: Builds the transfer clutch pack with dry frictions.
mistakes.consequence: The transfer frictions can scorch early and the clearance changes once they soak.
mistakes.prevent: Soak the transfer frictions in CVTF before stacking and measure with them soaked.

steps.title: Set transfer clutch clearance
steps.action: Measure transfer clutch clearance and use a different plate thickness until it is in range.
steps.mistake: Leaving the AWD clutch tight, which causes binding on tight turns.

mistakes.title: Transfer clutch pack too tight
mistakes.what: Leaves transfer clutch clearance below range.
mistakes.consequence: The AWD clutch binds on tight turns, scrubbing tires and overheating the pack.
mistakes.prevent: Change transfer plate thickness until clearance sits inside 0.7 to 1.1 mm.

mistakes.title: Transfer clutch pack too loose
mistakes.what: Accepts transfer clutch clearance above range.
mistakes.consequence: The rear axle gets torque late or weakly, and the transfer pack slips and glazes.
mistakes.prevent: Bring transfer clearance inside the range with a thicker plate before the air test.

steps.title: Air-test the transfer clutch
steps.action: Assemble drum and hub, hold them together in a press and apply shop air to the feed to watch the piston apply and release.
steps.why: The press stops the hub separating and tearing the sealing rings during the test.

mistakes.title: Air-testing outside the press
mistakes.what: Applies air to the transfer clutch without clamping drum and hub in a press.
mistakes.consequence: The air pushes the hub off the drum and cuts its sealing ring.
mistakes.prevent: Clamp the transfer drum and hub together in a press before applying air.

mistakes.title: Unregulated shop air
mistakes.what: Air-tests the transfer clutch at full line pressure.
mistakes.consequence: The piston slams over and its seals can be blown out of their grooves.
mistakes.prevent: Regulate the air to the stated 40 psi test pressure before touching the feed.

mistakes.title: Accepting a leaking apply
mistakes.what: Hears a hiss or a slow apply on the transfer clutch and carries on.
mistakes.consequence: The AWD clutch applies weakly and slips once the car is driven.
mistakes.prevent: Find and fix any transfer clutch leak while the assembly is still on the bench.

steps.title: Install the front differential
steps.action: Set the front differential into the converter case on its bearings.

mistakes.title: Differential bearings not seated
mistakes.what: Sets the differential in with a bearing race not fully home.
mistakes.consequence: Differential preload and backlash are off, and the final drive whines.
mistakes.prevent: Check both differential bearings sit fully in their bores before the pinion goes in.

steps.title: Install the pinion support
steps.action: Fit the pinion support with new seals, mesh the drive pinion with the differential gear and torque its bolts in a crossing pattern.
steps.why: If the hypoid gears, bearings or case were replaced, pinion depth and backlash must be re-set before going further.

mistakes.title: Rolled pinion support seal
mistakes.what: Fits the pinion support with a seal rolled, cut or missing.
mistakes.consequence: The support leaks where it should seal, and it sits under the case, so the case has to come off again.
mistakes.prevent: Lubricate the new support seals, check they sit in their grooves, and lower the support straight.

mistakes.title: Skipping depth and backlash checks
mistakes.what: Replaces the hypoid set, bearings or case but reuses the old setup.
mistakes.consequence: Gear mesh is wrong, so the final drive whines and the hypoid gears wear early.
mistakes.prevent: Re-set pinion depth and backlash whenever the hypoid set, its bearings or the case change.

mistakes.title: Pulling the support down unevenly
mistakes.what: Tightens the pinion support bolts one side at a time.
mistakes.consequence: The pinion support cocks in its bore, so pinion mesh and bearing load are both off.
mistakes.prevent: Tighten the fourteen support bolts in a crossing pattern in stages.

steps.title: Install the input shaft and drum
steps.action: Install the input shaft with the forward drum and clutch pack into the case.

mistakes.title: Cutting input rings entering bore
mistakes.what: Pushes the input shaft into its bore without rotating it.
mistakes.consequence: The input shaft sealing rings are cut and forward clutch pressure leaks.
